---
title: "Organize environment validators by feature"
description: "Keep validators under env/, reuse a base schema and inject one validated instance into the bot."
order: 4
category: "Environment"
---

## Give each set of variables a home

A small example can keep all its variables in one `app.env.ts`. As soon as a bot needs a database, an optional reporting endpoint, and a second deployment, it becomes easier to read if each piece has a place. Put the validator classes under `src/env/validators/` and let a concrete `AppEnv` collect the ones your process uses. The framework follows TypeScript inheritance from the class you pass to `EnvValidator.validate`. It doesn't scan folders for schemas.

## Build a schema from two, three or more groups

Start with the Discord settings in `SpraxiumBaseEnv`. `DatabaseEnv` extends that class to add MongoDB. For two feature groups, `ReportsEnv` extends `DatabaseEnv`. For a third, `CacheEnv` extends `ReportsEnv` and adds Redis. The diagram shows the full bot. Each validator lives in a separate file, and `AppEnv` is the only class the startup code needs to import.

~~~text
src/
  env/
    validators/
      database.env.ts
      reports.env.ts
      cache.env.ts
    app.env.ts
  app.module.ts
  main.ts
~~~

~~~ts filename="src/env/validators/database.env.ts"
import { Env, EnvSchema, IsMongoUri, Secret, SpraxiumBaseEnv } from '@spraxium/env';

@EnvSchema()
export class DatabaseEnv extends SpraxiumBaseEnv {
  @Env('MONGO_URI')
  @Secret()
  @IsMongoUri()
  mongoUri!: string;
}
~~~

~~~ts filename="src/env/validators/reports.env.ts"
import { Env, EnvSchema, IsBoolean, IsOptional, IsUrl, Secret } from '@spraxium/env';
import { DatabaseEnv } from './database.env';

@EnvSchema()
export class ReportsEnv extends DatabaseEnv {
  @Env('ENABLE_REPORTS', { default: 'false', secret: false })
  @IsBoolean()
  enableReports!: boolean;

  @Env('REPORTS_WEBHOOK_URL')
  @Secret()
  @IsOptional()
  @IsUrl({ https: true })
  reportsWebhookUrl?: string;
}
~~~

~~~ts filename="src/env/validators/cache.env.ts"
import { Env, EnvSchema, IsRedisUri, Secret } from '@spraxium/env';
import { ReportsEnv } from './reports.env';

@EnvSchema()
export class CacheEnv extends ReportsEnv {
  @Env('REDIS_URL')
  @Secret()
  @IsRedisUri()
  redisUrl!: string;
}
~~~

For a bot with just MongoDB, extend `DatabaseEnv` in `AppEnv`. To add reports, change that single `extends` to `ReportsEnv`. To add Redis too, use `CacheEnv`, as shown below. If you add a fourth group, put it in its own file, extend `CacheEnv` there, then point `AppEnv` at the new class. TypeScript allows one parent per class. Spraxium reads the `@Env` fields from that parent and every class above it, so you still call `EnvValidator.validate(AppEnv)` once.

~~~ts filename="src/env/app.env.ts"
import { EnvSchema } from '@spraxium/env';
import { CacheEnv } from './validators/cache.env';

@EnvSchema()
export class AppEnv extends CacheEnv {}
~~~

Set `MONGO_URI` in the bot environment and add `REDIS_URL` when you use `CacheEnv`. If you leave `ENABLE_REPORTS` out, its value is `false`. `REPORTS_WEBHOOK_URL` is optional. When you supply it, it must use HTTPS. If you want to require it only when reports are enabled, check those two values together when starting the reports service. The field decorators here check each variable on its own.

Keep the chain for settings that go together in this bot. If a separate worker only needs Redis, give it a `WorkerEnv` that declares its own `REDIS_URL` with the same decorators and validate it in the worker entry point. Extending the bot’s `CacheEnv` would also require the bot’s Discord and MongoDB settings. Give each feature its own property names and environment keys. This way, adding a class does not accidentally replace a setting from a parent class.

## Validate once, then inject the result

Read the environment before connecting to Discord. Register the value under the concrete `AppEnv` token. Services import `AppEnv` and use it as a dependency. A service shouldn't call `EnvValidator.validate` on every request or assume TypeScript converted a string read from `process.env`. Restart the service when its deployed environment changes. In development, an invalid startup can wait for an edit to the environment file. Outside development, validation errors stop the process.

~~~ts filename="src/main.ts"
import { IntentPreset, SpraxiumFactory } from '@spraxium/core';
import { EnvValidator } from '@spraxium/env';
import { AppEnv } from './env/app.env';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function main() {
  const env = EnvValidator.validate(AppEnv);
  const app = await SpraxiumFactory.create({ token: env.token });
  app.useModule(AppModule);
  app.provide(AppEnv, env);
  app.intents(IntentPreset.Standard);
  await app.listen();
}

void main();
~~~

~~~ts filename="src/modules/database/database.settings.ts"
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@spraxium/common';
import { AppEnv } from '../../env/app.env';

@Injectable()
export class DatabaseSettings {
  constructor(@Inject(AppEnv) private readonly env: AppEnv) {}

  get connectionUri(): string {
    return this.env.mongoUri;
  }
}
~~~

Register DatabaseSettings in the module that opens the database. Export the provider from that module when another feature genuinely needs the connection settings.

## Keep the configuration readable

Keep `.env` and `.env.local` out of Git and commit a `.env.example` with names and placeholders. The validator reads the first file it finds, with `.env.local` before `.env`, and initially leaves variables already set in the process alone. The folder for schema classes doesn't change where those files are loaded. `loadEnv({ path })` is separately available for a script that loads a custom path. In a test, give the process explicit values and use `silent: true` if you want to hide the success table. Errors still follow the usual exit or development behavior.
